profile.feeling: House and home at once — family, warmth, hospitality.

senses.def: home — فِي الْبَيْتِ (at home), إِلَى الْبَيْتِ (home, homewards)

examples.tr: This is my house.
Our house is big.
I am at home now.
I go back home in the evening.
This is a verse from a poem by al-Mutanabbī.
the people of the house (also: the Prophet’s family)

phrases.meaning: the heart of the matter, the main point

synonyms.nuance: house, residence — common in writing
house, abode — feminine; also in names: دَارُ النَّشْرِ (publishing house)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *bayt- (Wiktionary, which compares Amharic ቤት bēt); Hebrew בַּיִת (bayit) is the same word.

funFacts: The letter ב is called bet (“house”) in Hebrew, and Arabic ب is bāʾ: the old letter was a picture of a house.
Bethlehem is בֵּית לֶחֶם, “house of bread”, in Hebrew — in Arabic بَيْتُ لَحْمٍ reads as “house of meat”, because لَحْم means meat.
pitfalls: Two plurals, two meanings: بُيُوت = houses, أَبْيَات = verses of poetry.
بَيْت is masculine (الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ), while its synonym دَار is feminine.
subtleties: بَيْت is “home” too: فِي الْبَيْتِ = at home; أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ = the household.

profile.feeling: City life: a flat in a building, bought or rented.

examples.tr: We live in a small flat.
The flat is on the third floor.

examples.text: مِنْ مَعَانِي الشَّقَّةِ: الْقِسْمُ الْمُنْفَصِلُ مِنْ بِنَاءٍ أَوْ شَيْءٍ.
examples.tr: One of the meanings of šaqqa: a separate section of a building or of a thing.

synonyms.nuance: house, home — often used for one’s flat too
dwelling, residence (official language)

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no origin; the word belongs to the root ش ق ق (“to split, to divide”), like شِقّ (a half, a part).

funFacts: Its plural keeps the doubled root letter apart: شَقَّة → شُقَق (š-q-q).
pitfalls: Do not confuse شَقَّة (flat) with شِقَّة (a piece, a half) or شُقَّة (distance): the same letters, other vowels (Wiktionary lists all three).
subtleties: شَقَّةٌ لِلْإِيجَارِ = a flat for rent; شَقَّةٌ لِلْبَيْعِ = a flat for sale.

profile.feeling: A room of the house — and of hotels, offices, institutions.

examples.tr: This is the bedroom.
The room is big and clean.
the Chamber of Commerce and Industry

synonyms.nuance: room, chamber — more literary
room (from Turkish oda) — everyday Egyptian and Levantine

etymology.text: Root غ ر ف; Wiktionary gives no older origin. Through Andalusian Arabic it gave Old Spanish and Catalan algorfa (an attic, a granary), and Swahili ghorofa (storey).

funFacts: Swahili ghorofa (an upper floor) comes from غُرْفَة (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The usual plural is غُرَف (ġuraf); غُرُفَات / غُرْفَات also exist.
In “bedroom” the first noun has no article and the second has it: غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ — never *الْغُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ.
subtleties: Rooms are named by iḍāfa (noun + genitive): غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ = “room of the sleep”, غُرْفَةُ الْجُلُوسِ = sitting room.

profile.feeling: Door and gate — and, in books, a chapter.

senses.def: field, category; an opening, a chance

examples.tr: Open the door, please.
The door is closed.
I read the first chapter of the book.

synonyms.nuance: gate, gateway (large); also a web portal
entrance (the place, not the door itself)

etymology.text: Usually considered a borrowing from Aramaic בָּבָא (bāḇā, “gate”), from Akkadian bābum (“gate”); Hans Bauer considered it native (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Babylon is Akkadian Bāb-ilim, “gate of god” — the same word bāb.
Turkish bap (chapter) comes from بَاب in its sense “chapter” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The plural is أَبْوَاب: the hidden w of the root ب و ب appears.
بَاب is masculine: الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ (the door is open), not *مَفْتُوحَةٌ.
subtleties: A book’s أَبْوَاب are its chapters; فِي هٰذَا الْبَابِ = in this field.

profile.feeling: The standard written word for a window; speech prefers شُبَّاك.

senses.def: opening in a wall, air hole

examples.tr: Open the window, please.
The windows are open.
Close the window, it is cold.

synonyms.nuance: window — the everyday word in most dialects; also a ticket counter

etymology.text: From the root ن ف ذ, verb نَفَذَ (nafaḏa, “to pierce”): a word made in the late 19th century for “window” in literary Arabic (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A modern word: Wiktionary dates the meaning “window” to the late 19th century — before that, dialect words like شُبَّاك and طَاقَة were used.
pitfalls: The plural نَوَافِذ is a diptote: no tanwīn — نَوَافِذُ, نَوَافِذَ.
نَافِذَة is also the feminine of the adjective نَافِذ (in force): قَوَانِينُ نَافِذَةٌ (laws in force).
subtleties: In speech most Arabs say شُبَّاك; نَافِذَة sounds standard and written — and is the word on a computer screen.

profile.feeling: A solid wall — of a room, a house, a city; also figurative barriers.

examples.tr: There is a picture on the wall.
The wall of the room is white.

phrases.meaning: be careful what you say, someone may be listening

synonyms.nuance: wall — the everyday word; plural حِيطَان
an outer wall, a city wall, a fence

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares Hebrew גָּדֵר (gadér, “fence”), Phoenician gdr and Egyptian jmḏr.

funFacts: Hebrew גָּדֵר (gadér) means “fence” — the same old root, a lower wall (Wiktionary compares them).
pitfalls: Two plurals: جُدْرَان (usual) and جُدُر (literary).
جِدَار is masculine: الْجِدَارُ أَبْيَضُ — the adjective has the masculine form.
subtleties: جِدَار is a little more formal and figurative; حَائِط is everyday — the Western Wall is حَائِطُ الْمَبْكَى or حَائِطُ الْبُرَاقِ.

profile.feeling: The table of everyday life — and the board of backgammon in the café.

examples.tr: The books are on the table.
We booked a table for two.
My grandfather plays backgammon at the café.

synonyms.nuance: (dining) table, a table laid with food — literary
desk; also office
table — everyday Egyptian word

etymology.text: From Italian tavola (“table”), from Latin tabula; reshaped to the native pattern فَاعِلَة, possibly by phono-semantic matching with the root ط و ل (“long”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its second meaning, backgammon, links it to Turkish tavla and Greek τάβλι — all from Latin tabula, a board.
pitfalls: A loanword that follows Arabic rules: feminine with ة, sound plural طَاوِلَات.
مَائِدَة is a table laid with food (and the name of a sura, سُورَةُ الْمَائِدَةِ); for the piece of furniture say طَاوِلَة.
subtleties: “To play backgammon” is لَعِبَ الطَّاوِلَةَ — the same word as the table.

profile.feeling: An ordinary chair — and, in high style, a throne or a professor’s chair.

examples.tr: Sit on the chair.
This chair is comfortable.
the Throne Verse (Qurʾān 2:255)

examples.text: يَشْغَلُ أُسْتَاذُنَا الْكُرْسِيَّ الْوَحِيدَ لِلْفَلْسَفَةِ فِي الْجَامِعَةِ.
examples.tr: Our professor holds the only chair of philosophy at the university.

synonyms.nuance: seat (in a car, bus, theatre, parliament)
throne

etymology.text: Thought to be borrowed from Aramaic כּוּרְסְיָא (kursəyā); compare Biblical Hebrew כִּסֵּא (kissé), Akkadian kussûm — ultimately from Sumerian guza, “chair” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish kürsü (lectern, podium) and Malay and Indonesian kursi (chair) come from it (Wiktionary).
The chain goes back to Sumerian guza — one of the oldest traceable words in this course.
pitfalls: The ending is a doubled yā: كُرْسِيّ (kursiyy); with the article الْكُرْسِيُّ.
The plural كَرَاسِيّ is a diptote (كَرَاسِيُّ, no tanwīn); it is usually written simply كراسي.
subtleties: آيَةُ الْكُرْسِيِّ, the Throne Verse, is one of the best-known verses of the Qurʾān — there كُرْسِيّ is God’s throne.

profile.feeling: The bed (the piece of furniture); rest, sleep — and in hospitals, capacity.

examples.tr: The bed is in the bedroom.

synonyms.nuance: bedding, mattress; the bed one lies in (مَرِيضٌ فِي الْفِرَاشِ)
bed (from Persian)

etymology.text: Root س ر ر; Wiktionary gives no older origin.

funFacts: The same root gives سُرُور (joy) and سِرّ (secret).
pitfalls: Plural أَسِرَّة, with a doubled r: الْأَسِرَّةُ.
Sun letter: with the article the s is doubled — السَّرِيرُ (as-sarīr).
subtleties: As in English, hospitals count beds: مُسْتَشْفًى بِمِئَةِ سَرِيرٍ (a hundred-bed hospital).

examples.tr: The clothes are in the wardrobe.

synonyms.nuance: cupboard, wardrobe — very common in speech (Egypt, Gulf)

etymology.text: Root خ ز ن (“to store”); Wiktionary gives no older origin. It passed into Classical Persian (خِزَانَه).

funFacts: English magazine and German Magazin come from the Arabic plural مَخَازِن (storehouses), of the same root خ ز ن, through Italian magazzino.
pitfalls: Spelled with kasra: خِزَانَة (ḫizāna); خَزِينَة is another word (treasury, cash box).
The plural خَزَائِن is a diptote; the sound plural خِزَانَات is also used.
subtleties: Literally “a place of storing”: the same root gives مَخْزَن (warehouse) and خَزْن (storage).

etymology.text: Tool noun from the root ص ب ح (ṣ b ḥ); compare صَبْح (ṣabḥ, “dawn”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: مِصْبَاح and صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ share the root ص ب ح (“dawn, morning”).
pitfalls: The plural مَصَابِيح is a diptote: no tanwīn (مَصَابِيحُ).
The pattern مِفْعَال names tools: مِصْبَاح (lamp), مِفْتَاح (key) — learn them together.
subtleties: The light itself is ضَوْء or نُور; مِصْبَاح is the device that gives it.

profile.feeling: The book — and, in high style, the written word, a letter, the Scripture.

examples.tr: This is a new book.
I am reading a book about the history of Egypt.
The books are on the shelf.
the People of the Book (Jews and Christians)
Your letter reached me yesterday and I was glad of it.

phrases.tr: and the best companion at any time is a book

synonyms.nuance: a (written) work, a publication
booklet, brochure (diminutive)

etymology.text: From the root ك ت ب (“writing”): Wiktionary lists it as the verbal noun of كَتَبَ (kataba, “to write”) as well as “book”.

funFacts: Turkish kitap, Persian and Hindi kitāb, Swahili kitabu: all from كِتَاب (Wiktionary lists dozens of descendants).
Hebrew כְּתָב (ktav, script, writing) has the same root k-t-b.
pitfalls: The plural is كُتُب (kutub) — كِتَابَات means “writings”.
Unvocalized كتاب can also be كُتَّاب (writers, plural of كَاتِب) — the vowels and the šadda decide.
subtleties: One root, a whole family: كَتَبَ (he wrote), كَاتِب (writer), مَكْتَب (desk, office), مَكْتَبَة (library, bookshop), مَكْتُوب (written).

senses.def: handwriting, style; “by the pen of” (an author)

examples.tr: Do you have a pen?

an article by (lit. by the pen of) the writer

phrases.meaning: from the first revealed sura: God taught mankind by the pen

synonyms.nuance: a quill; an artist’s brush; a writer’s pen (figurative)

etymology.text: Derived from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”), perhaps through Geʿez ቀለም (ḳäläm) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: From Greek κάλαμος, “reed” — the first pens were cut reeds. Turkish kalem and Swahili kalamu come from the Arabic (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: قَلَم covers pens and pencils; a pencil is قَلَمُ رَصَاصٍ.
The plural has a hamza: أَقْلَام, الْأَقْلَامُ.
subtleties: بِقَلَمِ فُلَانٍ under an article = “written by so-and-so” (Wiktionary).

synonyms.nuance: paper, a sheet — a classical word

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *waraḳ- (“leaf”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish varak (a thin leaf, gold leaf) comes from وَرَق (Wiktionary).
Stuffed vine leaves are وَرَقُ عِنَبٍ — the same word as paper.
pitfalls: وَرَق is the material (a collective, masculine); one sheet is وَرَقَة (feminine); several sheets أَوْرَاق.
أَوْرَاق often means “papers, documents”: أَوْرَاقُ السَّفَرِ (travel documents).
subtleties: لَعِبَ الْوَرَقَ = to play cards: the cards are “the paper”.

profile.feeling: The standard written word for “telephone”; speech says تِلِفُون, مُوبَايِل, جَوَّال.

senses.def: a voice calling out (an unseen caller)

examples.tr: The phone is ringing.

He heard a voice calling in the night.

synonyms.nuance: telephone — the international word, everyday
mobile phone
mobile phone

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of the verb هَتَفَ (hatafa, “to shout, to call out”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its old meaning (Wiktionary) is “a voice calling out” — a fitting name for the telephone.
pitfalls: The plural هَوَاتِف is a diptote: هَوَاتِفُ, no tanwīn.
In speech you mostly hear تِلِفُون, مُوبَايِل, جَوَّال or مَحْمُول; هَاتِف is the written standard.
subtleties: “To phone someone” is usually اِتَّصَلَ بِـ (to connect with); the verb هَاتَفَ (to telephone) also exists (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: The opener — of doors, of problems, of happiness.

senses.def: key (to a problem); legend (of a map)

examples.tr: Where is the house key?
I forgot the key in the car.
the keyboard
Patience is the key to relief.

phrases.tr: patience is the key to relief
phrases.meaning: be patient and things will get better

profile.synonymsNone: No real synonym in MSA; مُفْتَاح (with u) is the spoken pronunciation in Egypt, the Hejaz and Morocco (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: Tool noun (pattern مِفْعَال) from the verb فَتَحَ (fataḥa, “to open”); Wiktionary compares Hebrew מַפְתֵּחַ (maftéakh).

funFacts: Hebrew מַפְתֵּחַ (maftéakh, key) is built the same way from the same root (Wiktionary).
الْفَاتِحَة, “the Opener” — the first sura of the Qurʾān — has the same root ف ت ح.
pitfalls: The plural مَفَاتِيح is a diptote: مَفَاتِيحُ, no tanwīn.
Pattern مِفْعَال = a tool: مِفْتَاح is literally “an opener”.
subtleties: مِفْتَاحُ الْخَرِيطَةِ is the legend of a map; مِفْتَاحُ الْحَلِّ the key to the solution.

profile.feeling: Bags of every kind — school bag, handbag, suitcase — and a minister’s portfolio.

examples.tr: The bag is very heavy.
I put the books in the bag.
He took over the foreign-affairs portfolio.

synonyms.nuance: bag, suitcase — the everyday word (from Turkish çanta)
a (plastic or paper) bag, a sack

etymology.text: Root ح ق ب; Wiktionary gives no older origin. It passed into Ottoman Turkish (Turkish heybe, “saddlebag”), Albanian and Armenian.

funFacts: Turkish heybe (saddlebag) comes from حَقِيبَة, while the Arabic everyday word شَنْطَة comes from Turkish çanta: a loan in each direction.
pitfalls: The plural حَقَائِب is a diptote: حَقَائِبُ.
A plastic shopping bag is كِيس, not حَقِيبَة.
subtleties: وَزِيرٌ بِلَا حَقِيبَةٍ = a minister without portfolio.

root.none: a loanword (Persian, from Greek): no Arabic root

profile.feeling: A small cup of coffee or tea — hospitality in miniature.

examples.tr: A cup of coffee, please.
I drank two cups of tea.
She read his coffee cup (his fortune in the grounds).

phrases.meaning: a storm in a teacup — a big fuss about nothing

synonyms.nuance: cup, mug or glass — bigger, often without a saucer
a glass, a goblet; also a trophy

etymology.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian پِنْگَان (pingān), possibly from Syriac and Aramaic פִּינְכָא (pīnəkā), from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “plate, board”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek φλιτζάνι (cup) comes from Turkish fincan, from this Arabic word — which itself goes back through Persian and Aramaic to Greek πίναξ: a round trip.
pitfalls: The plural فَنَاجِين is a diptote: فَنَاجِينُ.
فِنْجَان is masculine though small and dainty: فِنْجَانٌ صَغِيرٌ.
subtleties: فِنْجَان is the small cup for Arabic or Turkish coffee (or tea); a big mug is كُوب.

profile.feeling: A glass or goblet — water, a toast, or the cup of victory.

examples.tr: A glass of water, please.
This glass is clean.
France won the World Cup.

collocations.tr: to raise the glass (or the cup)

synonyms.nuance: glass, cup, mug — masculine; very common for a glass of water

etymology.text: Perhaps from Proto-Semitic *kaʔs-; Wiktionary also considers a later borrowing from Aramaic.

funFacts: Hebrew כּוֹס (kos, cup, glass) is the related word — and it is feminine in Hebrew too.
pitfalls: كَأْس is feminine although it has no ة: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ، الْكَأْسُ نَظِيفَةٌ.
The plural كُؤُوس has its hamza on a wāw: الْكُؤُوسُ.
subtleties: In literature كَأْس is often the wine cup — and one’s fate: كَأْسُ الْمَوْتِ, the cup of death.

profile.feeling: The plate on the table — and the open courtyard of a mosque.

examples.tr: The plates are on the table.
I ate a plate of rice.
This plate is clean.
the courtyard of the mosque

synonyms.nuance: plate, dish — also a dish on a menu

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic, related to the root ص ف ح; akin to Geʿez ጻሕል (ṣaḥl, “bowl”) and Hebrew צַלַּחַת (tsalákhat, “plate, dish”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek σαγάνι (a shallow pan) — and the dish σαγανάκι named after it — comes from Turkish sahan, from Arabic صَحْن (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The plural is صُحُون: غَسَلْتُ الصُّحُونَ (I washed the dishes).
Sun letter: with the article the ṣ is doubled — الصَّحْنُ.
subtleties: The plate is صَحْن; the food on the menu is طَبَق: الطَّبَقُ الرَّئِيسِيُّ = the main course.
